accuracy.evidence: Thick, air-trapping materials slow heat moving in or out (thermal insulation); a coat keeps body heat in and makes none; wrapping slows cooling but never raises a drink above its starting temperature; wrapping keeps cold things cold. Checked against Development Matters (2021) Understanding the World and the National Curriculum Year 2 'uses of everyday materials'. Lab model checked by hand: the bare cube loses 25% a wait and the socked cube 8%, so the bare one is gone after 4 waits with the socked cube 68% left; wrappers rank scarf 0.8 > tissue 0.45 > net 0.25; cocoa warmth 1 - 0.8/(1+L) gives 0.2, 0.6, 0.73, 0.8 for 0-3 layers against the 0.7 line, so 2 layers is the first pass and no value exceeds 1. The 6 sort cards were each checked (flask, blanket and tea towel keep warm; cool bag, cool box and towel round ice keep cold). The numbers are a qualitative model, not measured minutes, and the text never claims times.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the heat ideas documented by Erickson (1979) and summarised in Driver and others (1994): wool or a coat makes heat (ice race predict, snowman feedback, p5, m3, m6, challenge 'woolhot'), wrapping makes things hotter than they started (layers predict and bell feedback, m2, challenge 'hotter'), wrapping only works for warm things (sort predict and feedback, m1, m8, challenge 'onlywarm'), any wrapper works (cups feedback for tissue and net, p4, m7, challenge 'thin') and only cloth keeps warm (m5, challenge 'cloth').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagwrap is about heat moving through a wrapper: an ice cube shrinks with a growing puddle while its socked twin barely changes, three wrapped cups show thermometer bars that fall by different amounts, a cup's bar must stay above a dashed playtime line as layers are added and never rises above full, wraps are sorted by keeping warmth in or out, and warmth dots escape from a child's uncovered head, neck and body until the hat, scarf and coat go on (and the coat is refused for the snowman). None of this transfers to another topic by relabelling.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child runs each test before the rule is stated: the 'which melted first' tap is locked until the bare cube is all water, the warmest-cup tap is locked until all three wrappers are on and time has passed, and the playtime bell rejects 0 and 1 layer with 'cooled too much, add another layer'. Wrong taps name the slip (the sock kept the warm air out; the net has big holes; a coat will not warm the snowman), and the done messages only confirm what the scene showed.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 'The one in the sock' melts first (the bare cube melts first), 'Yes, wrapping adds heat' (the bar only falls, slowest with more layers), 'It melts faster, towels are warm' for an ice lolly in a towel (the towel card belongs in Stays cold), and 'The coat makes it' for the warmth inside a coat (warmth dots come from the child's body and the snowman gets none).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions whose wrong options carry five tagged messages: woolhot (wool and coats do not make heat), onlywarm (wrapping keeps cold things cold too), thin (thick fluffy wrapping traps air; thin or holey wrapping lets heat through), hotter (wrapping cannot make things hotter than they started) and cloth (bubble wrap and foam trap air too). Answer order rotates per question.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences about socks, hats, scarves and ice cream, with one idea each; lab prompts give one action at a time. Terms like insulation, properties of materials and National Curriculum stay in the adult text; the validator's kid and adult readability limits pass.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs: the sock test, the hat keeps your warmth in, thick beats thin, wrapping keeps cold things cold and never adds heat. Adult paragraphs: curriculum placement, two home tests, four named mistakes with research, what each lab scene does. The content gate's filler and 12% duplicate checks pass.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360 px screenshots in light and dark: the two ice cubes and their plates sit side by side with the sock and a 50%-width Wait key below, three cups narrowed to 17% of the width so each thermometer fits beside its cup, the layered cup and tall playtime thermometer share a row, sort cards sit in a 3 x 2 grid with 12 px two-line labels, and the child, snowman and clothes column fit without clipping. The iPhone 13 walkthrough completes every Show me.

accessibility.evidence: Each canvas action has a labelled button twin: Sock on cube 1 or 2, Wait, Cube N melted first; each wrapper to each cup, Wait, Cup N is warmest; Add a layer, Take a layer off, Wait for playtime; each card to warm or cold; each clothing item to the child or the snowman. The canvas aria-label reports every count, bar and verdict in words; axe WCAG 2.1 AA runs clean in light and dark themes.
